title: MUSE stellar kinematics give the ASASSN-14ko black hole about 10^7.6 solar masses, below the 10^8.2 that a light-travel-time clock needs; with this mass the flare timing no longer prefers that clock
abstract: Question: a light-travel-time (Roemer) clock can stop the period decrease of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko without an orbital change, and SCI 8e6f3b54 found a Bayes factor of about e^2 for it, but only if the central black hole has log10 M >= 8.2. Is the mass this high, and do archival flare spectra show the predicted line velocities? Data: the public MUSE cube of 2015 (ESO), nine PESSTO spectra of 2014-2015 and 28 HST/STIS UV spectra of 2020-2021, not used before in the campaign. Results: (1) pPXF fits of the Ca II triplet and Mg b outside the AGN light give a stellar velocity dispersion of 123 +/- 10 km/s (72 variants: 107-133 km/s). M-sigma relations give log10 M = 7.56 +/- 0.33 (Kormendy & Ho 2013) or 7.12 +/- 0.43 (McConnell & Ma 2013). log10 M = 8.19 needs 171-190 km/s. (2) The timing alone needs log10 M = 8.31-9.92 (95%). (3) We repeated the nested sampling of 8e6f3b54 with the new mass priors: the ln Bayes factor of the Roemer clock against a constant period derivative falls from +2.25 (host prior) to +0.46 (KH13) and -1.39 (MM13); a reweighting check gives +1.43, -0.63 and -2.06. (4) The 2014 broad H-beta excess (+300 to +400 km/s) persists after the continuum returned to baseline, so it is an echo of the AGN broad-line region and cannot test the clock. (5) The transient UV troughs at the 2020 flare rise (-2200 to -2800 km/s) sit at the velocities of narrow absorbers present in the quiescent 2021 spectra (N V -2000 km/s), so they are most simply a persistent AGN absorber seen against the flare light. (6) The 1-arcsec PESSTO slit includes the companion nucleus by an amount that depends on slit angle; the earlier 10^8.18 broad-line mass used a flare-echo spectrum. Conclusion: the first dynamical mass is about 10^7.6 solar masses; with it, the flare timing no longer prefers a light-travel-time clock, so an orbital or emission-geometry cause of the stall is more probable. Limitations: M-sigma scatter of 0.3-0.4 dex in a disturbed two-nucleus host; aperture dispersions, not sigma_e; no virial mass; no flare-intrinsic emission line, so no direct kinematic test; absolute ln Z differs by about 1 between methods.

display.caption: Left: the black-hole mass that the light-travel-time (Roemer) clock needs from the 2014-2026 flare timing alone (grey, log10 M = 8.31-9.92) against the host prior of Payne et al. (2021) and the two dynamical priors from the MUSE stellar dispersion (log10 M = 7.56 and 7.12). Right: the ln Bayes factor of the Roemer clock against a constant period derivative falls from +2.3 to +0.5 (KH13) and -1.4 (MM13).

MUSE stellar kinematics of the ASASSN-14ko host: apertures with the companion nucleus masked, pPXF fits of the Ca II triplet and Mg b in the 1.5-5 arcsec annulus, and the dispersion against aperture. All apertures outside the AGN give 112-130 km/s, far below the 171 km/s that log10 M = 8.19 needs.

HST/STIS N V, C IV and Si IV: the broad troughs at the 2020 December flare rise (blue) lie at the velocities of narrow absorbers that are present in the 2021 quiescent spectra (black, grey), so they are most simply a persistent AGN absorber seen against the flare light.

citations.reason: We use its 61 flare markers, its Roemer timing library and its sampler set-up. Our dynamical mass removes its e^2 Bayes factor for the light-travel-time clock; we answer its request for a mass or line-velocity test.
